what-ai-and-ml-are.title: Welcome to What AI and machine learning really are, part of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML).
what-ai-and-ml-are.idea: Two failures are equally common. One is dismissing AI as a fad, which means missing tools that genuinely change what a small team can build. The other is believing the marketing, which leads to systems deployed on work they cannot do — medical judgement, legal advice, hiring decisions — with consequences for real people. The way out of both is precise vocabulary and an accurate mental model of what a model is.
what-ai-and-ml-are.example: Task: classify incoming customer support messages into five categories so they reach the right queue. Rules. Keyword lists per category. A day to build, transparent, no data needed. It handles 60% of messages and fails on anything phrased unexpectedly — which is exactly the messages that matter, because unusual phrasing often signals unusual problems. It is also a maintenance burden: every new phrasing is a new rule. Supervised classification. Label 2,000 historical messages, train a model (a linear classifier or a small transformer), measure accuracy on a held-out set. If it reaches 88% overall but 61% on the rarest and most important category ("payment problems"), the average is not the number to deploy on. You would collect more examples of that category, or route it to a human and say so. A language model with a prompt and a taxonomy. No training data, minutes to prototype, and it can explain its choice. It is more expensive per message, less deterministic, and needs guarding: it will confidently mislabel, and it must never be the component that decides whether a refund is approved. Used as a first-pass router with confidence thresholds and human review for the uncertain cases, it is often the best value for a small team — because the alternative is weeks of labelling nobody has time for. The honest conclusion is neither "use AI" nor "use rules": each approach has a measurable cost, a measurable error rate and a different failure mode, and the choice belongs to whoever owns the consequences of a mistake.
what-ai-and-ml-are.challenge: Write a two-page assessment of one real task in an organisation you know — sorting applications, predicting demand, answering common questions — stating the decision it affects, the data that exists today, the measurable objective, the cost of a false positive versus a false negative, the three approaches (rules, trained model, prompted model) with estimated cost and accuracy, and a recommendation with the fallback for when the system is wrong.

the-machine-learning-workflow.title: Welcome to The machine learning workflow, part of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML).
the-machine-learning-workflow.idea: "We have data, let us apply machine learning" is the sentence that begins most abandoned projects. The alternative order is unglamorous and works: decide what prediction would change what decision, find out whether the data can support it, build the simplest baseline, measure it against the cost of being wrong, then improve only what the measurement justifies.
the-machine-learning-workflow.example: A subscription business wants to predict which customers will cancel so that somebody can call them. The first attempt reports 99.4% accuracy. It is worthless, and the reasons are instructive. First, the classes are imbalanced: 1.8% of customers cancel in a given month. A model that always predicts "stays" scores 98.2% and is useless. Accuracy was the wrong metric from the start; precision, recall and the confusion matrix are the right ones, because the cost of a missed churner (lost revenue) differs sharply from the cost of a false alarm (a wasted call). Second, leakage: the feature supportticketaboutcancellation was populated after* the customer decided to leave. It predicts churn with near-perfect fidelity and is unavailable at prediction time. Removing it drops the score to something honest. Third, the split was random over time, so the model trained on July and was tested on March — reading the future. A time-based split gives the real number. Fourth, the target was undefined: "cancel" meant account closure in one table and non-renewal in another, and the two disagreed for 400 customers. Fixing the definition changed the label for 8% of the dataset. After all four repairs the model reports 71% recall at 45% precision. That is a modest, honest, useful result: it finds seven of ten people who will leave, at the cost of calling roughly one customer in two who was never going to. The business can decide whether that trade is worth a retention call — which is the only question that ever mattered.
the-machine-learning-workflow.challenge: Take one real prediction problem end to end: frame it, define the target, explore the data's coverage and gaps, split it by time, beat a baseline with a simple model, evaluate with cost-weighted metrics, inspect and explain the errors rather than the score, and write a one-page deployment plan with monitoring, retraining cadence and a kill switch. Report honestly where the model is weak, and what you would collect to fix it.

neural-networks-and-generative-ai.title: Welcome to Neural networks and generative AI, part of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML).
neural-networks-and-generative-ai.idea: You do not need to be able to implement backpropagation to build with models competently — but you do need enough of a mental model to predict where they will be strong, where they will fail, and what governs their cost. This lesson provides exactly that: mechanics in plain language, then the engineering patterns that turn a model into a dependable feature.
neural-networks-and-generative-ai.example: A training provider wants an assistant that answers questions about fees, schedules and policies. The naive version — a system prompt with the whole policy pasted in — works in a demo and fails in production: outdated text is baked into the prompt, answers cite nothing, and the model invents a fee when the question is slightly unusual. The production design has five parts. Ingestion: documents are chunked, embedded and stored with source metadata. Retrieval: the question is embedded, the top passages are fetched, and a cheap re-ranking step removes irrelevant ones. Grounding: the model is instructed to answer only from the retrieved passages, to say "I could not find this in the policy documents" when it cannot, and to cite the document and section. Guardrails: no fee changes, no medical or legal advice, and a handoff to a human for anything the retriever scores poorly. Measurement: a 120-case test set scored on factual accuracy, citation presence and refusal correctness, plus cost and latency tracking. The results illustrate the pattern: accuracy on in-scope questions rises from 68% to 94%, invented answers fall to near zero, and the assistant refuses or escalates 11% of questions — a feature, not a failure. The cost is a few cents per conversation, dominated by retrieval and the escalation path rather than the model call.
neural-networks-and-generative-ai.challenge: Build a small grounded assistant over documents you own: ingestion with chunking and metadata, retrieval with re-ranking, a grounded prompt with citation and refusal instructions, guardrails on cost and actions, and a scored test set of at least 40 cases including adversarial ones. Report accuracy, citation rate, correct-refusal rate, cost per conversation and p95 latency — and write down the two cases where it is still unreliable.

ethics-and-deploying-ai-responsibly.title: Welcome to Ethics, risk and deploying AI responsibly, part of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML).
ethics-and-deploying-ai-responsibly.idea: AI systems are now used for credit decisions, hiring screens, medical triage, exam marking and benefit eligibility — decisions that change lives. The difference between a toy and a system that affects people is accountability: somebody must be able to explain what it does, show what it does badly, and be answerable when it is wrong. That is a professional obligation as much as a legal one.
ethics-and-deploying-ai-responsibly.example: A lender wants to use a model to pre-screen loan applications. The model performs well on average (AUC 0.78) and the team is ready to ship. A responsible review changes the plan in four ways. Per-subgroup evaluation. Accuracy is measured separately for gender, age band, region and loan size. It reveals that recall for applicants under 25 is 0.61 against 0.79 for everyone else: young applicants with good creditworthiness are being rejected more often. That is a harm, and it is invisible in the average. Proxy features. residentialpostcode and devicetype are strong predictors and correlate closely with income and with region. Their inclusion hard-codes historical exclusion: a neighbourhood that was under-served by banks looks risky because it was under-served. Both are removed, at a cost of a few points of AUC that the team accepts. Explainability and contestability. Every declined applicant receives the three factors that mattered most and a route to a human review. The model is therefore chosen partly for how explainable it is, which is a legitimate engineering constraint — a slightly less accurate logistic model that can explain itself is better than an unexplainable one for a consequential decision. Governance. The model is documented with its intended use, its training data window, its measured subgroup performance and its known limitations. It is reviewed quarterly, monitored for drift, and it never makes the final decision: it produces a recommendation with a value, and a human or a policy rule makes the call. The audit trail records the model version, the inputs and the outcome for each decision, because a decision that cannot be reconstructed cannot be defended.
ethics-and-deploying-ai-responsibly.challenge: Conduct a responsible-deployment review for one system you have built, or a real one you can study: the decisions it affects, who bears the harms, per-subgroup results, proxy features and what you removed, the explanation a person receives, the appeal path, the data governance, the monitoring, and the named owner. Present it as a two-page review with recommendations — and state honestly which recommendation you would refuse to ship without.
